proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary finite scenario list
\(\mathcal H_0=\{h^1,\ldots,h^M\}\subset[-H,H]^K\).  Only finiteness and
\(|h_j^m|\leq H\) are used below.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), define the vertex control
\[
 u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\tag{1}
\]
The randomization producing \(A_i\) is made at the left endpoint from
\(\mathcal F_{i-1}\).  Thus (1) is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\), and it is an element of
\(\mathcal U\) by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}continuous\mbox{-}observed\mbox{-}control}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\).  Conditional on
the past and \(A_i=j\), the diffusion increments are
\[
 \Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
 +W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
 \sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{n},\frac1n\right),
 \qquad \Delta Q_j=\frac1n,
\tag{2}
\]
and all other coordinates have zero increments.  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}known\mbox{-}variance}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}local\mbox{-}scenario\mbox{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\), conditional on the same history and action, has the score
law in (2).  Induction over \(i\) proves equality of the complete observed
score--clock laws under every scenario \(m\).  Consequently every finite
policy is embedded exactly as a vertex-control diffusion policy, with the
same scenario-risk vector.

\emph{Continuous-payoff approximation.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be continuous, for
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We first prove that its prior-weighted value over
\(n\)-grid vertex controls converges to its value over \(\mathcal U\).
On the canonical observed space, a progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control \(u\) can be approximated by simple
predictable controls \(u^{(r)}\): approximate bounded predictable
coordinates by simple predictable functions and project their vectors onto
the closed simplex.  Bounded convergence in measure then gives
\[
 \mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j
 |u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{3}
\]
The elementary inequality
\((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\leq |a-b|\), for \(a,b\geq0\), and Itô isometry show
from (3) that the martingale parts of the score vectors converge in
\(L^2(\mathbb P_0)\); the clock vectors converge in \(L^1(\mathbb P_0)\).
Since \(|h_j^m|\leq H\), the drift terms converge in \(L^1\) under every
scenario as well.

For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its finitely many time cells
into \(n\)-grid cells.  At the left endpoint of a grid cell, choose vertex
\(j\) with the simplex probabilities prescribed by the simple control.
For each time cell, the sum of the conditional variances of the normalized
centered allocation counts is at most the reciprocal of the number of grid
cells, and hence tends to zero.  Conditional on those counts, the coordinate
score increment has mean \(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\) and variance \(\Delta Q_j\);
its characteristic function is
\[
 \exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
 -\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\}.
\tag{4}
\]
At the finitely many decision times, each past-measurable action kernel can
be replaced by one continuous outside a set of arbitrarily small
\(\mathbb P_0\)-probability: on the finite-dimensional Gaussian history
space, approximate its bounded coordinate functions by continuous functions
off a small Borel set and project back onto the simplex.  A union bound over
the finitely many cells controls the probability that the replacement
changes any action.  Induction over the cells can therefore apply (4) at
continuity points.  Letting the exceptional probability vanish, and then
using the approximation in (3), yields a diagonal sequence of predictable
grid policies \(\pi_n[u]\) for which
\[
 (X_n,Q_n)\Longrightarrow(X^u(1),Q^u(1))
 \quad\text{under the zero-drift reference law}.
\tag{5}
\]
The vertex randomization allows a simplex coordinate to equal zero; no
positive allocation lower bound has been introduced.

We now transfer (5) to every declared scenario without treating the adaptive
clock as independent of the score.  Under the zero-drift reference law put
\[
 M_m(t)=\sum_jh_j^m\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),
 \qquad
 A_m(t)=\langle M_m\rangle_t
 =\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t).
\tag{6}
\]
Because \(\sum_jQ_j(1)=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\),
\[
 0\leq A_m(1)\leq H^2.
\tag{7}
\]
The likelihood ratio from the zero-drift law to scenario \(m\) is
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))
 =\exp\{M_m(1)-\tfrac12A_m(1)\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Its square factors pathwise as
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2
 =\underbrace{\exp\{2M_m(1)-2A_m(1)\}}_
 {\mathcal E(2M_m)_1}\exp\{A_m(1)\}.
\tag{9}
\]
This is a factorization, not an independence assertion.  Moreover,
\[
 \frac12\langle2M_m\rangle_1=2A_m(1)\leq2H^2.
\tag{10}
\]
We verify the needed mean-one property rather than assume it.  If the
integrand of \(2M_m\) is simple predictable, successive conditioning uses
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[
 e^{\beta\Delta W-\beta^2\Delta t/2}\mid\mathcal F_{\mathrm{left}}
 \right]=1
\]
for every past-measurable \(\beta\), and hence
\(\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1=1\).  For a general progressively
measurable control, approximate the bounded integrand in
\(L^2(dt\,d\mathbb P_0)\) by simple predictable integrands.  The stochastic
integrals and brackets then converge in probability.  For every simple
approximant \(R\) with energy at most \(4H^2\), the same factorization and
conditional-Gaussian calculation at the doubled integrand give
\[
 \mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(R)_1^2]
 =\mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(2R)_1e^{\langle R\rangle_1}]
 \leq e^{4H^2}.
\]
Thus these exponentials are uniformly integrable, so passage to the limit
preserves their mean one.  Combining this bounded-energy conclusion with
the pointwise bound (7) in (9) gives the corrected estimate
\[
 \mathbb E_0[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2]
 \leq e^{H^2}\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1
 =e^{H^2}.
\tag{11}
\]
The same calculation holds for grid vertex controls: the corresponding
piecewise-constant stochastic integral has bracket
\(\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_{j,n}\leq H^2\).  Thus the family of likelihood ratios
for the approximating controls is uniformly integrable.  Since
\[
 Z_m(x,q)=
 \exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mx_j-\frac12
 \sum_j(h_j^m)^2q_j\right\}
\tag{12}
\]
is continuous, truncation of \(Z_m\), (5), and the uniform \(L^2\) bound
(11) imply
\[
 \mathbb E_m^{\pi_n[u]}g_m(X_n,Q_n)
 =\mathbb E_0^{\pi_n[u]}[Z_m(X_n,Q_n)g_m(X_n,Q_n)]
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))g_m(X(1),Q(1))]
 =\mathbb E_m^ug_m(X(1),Q(1)).
\tag{13}
\]
Because \(M\) is finite, the convergence holds simultaneously for all
scenarios.

Let \(G_n(\lambda)\) and \(G(\lambda)\) denote the infimal
prior-weighted risks for the continuous payoffs \(g_m\), over
\(\Pi_n\) and \(\mathcal U\), respectively.  Exact embedding gives
\(G(\lambda)\leq G_n(\lambda)\) for every \(n\).  Conversely, choose a
control within an arbitrary positive tolerance of \(G(\lambda)\) and apply
(13); hence \(\limsup_nG_n(\lambda)\leq G(\lambda)\).  Therefore
\[
 G_n(\lambda)\longrightarrow G(\lambda).
\tag{14}
\]

For fixed \(\delta>0\), the envelope losses specified in
\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite arithmetic means, finite minima, and
\(f_\delta^\pm\) are continuous.  Equation (14) gives
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)
 \longrightarrow B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda).
\tag{15}
\]
For either sign and either experiment, the value is
\(1\)-Lipschitz in \(\lambda\) under the \(\ell_1\) norm, since every
scenario loss lies in \([0,1]\).  A finite \(\ell_1\)-net of compact
\(\Delta_M\), followed by the two Lipschitz inequalities, upgrades (15) to
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)-B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{16}
\]

\emph{Removal of the envelopes.}
The pointwise scalar inequalities
\(f_\delta^-\leq\mathbf1\{\,\cdot<0\,\}\leq f_\delta^+\) and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) give
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
 B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),\qquad
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq
 B_\delta^+(\lambda),
\tag{17}
\]
and bound each upper-minus-lower width by
\(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta)\), uniformly in \(n\) and \(\lambda\).
Combining (16)--(17), with \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), yields
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \leq \rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\tag{18}
\]
The last assertion of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) permits
\(\delta\downarrow0\), and therefore
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{19}
\]
For the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Consequently
\[
 \max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]

It remains to transfer the minimax regret.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable finite-experiment regret vectors.  Exogenous
randomization at time zero makes \(C_n\) convex, and it is compact by
closure in the compact cube.  If
\(v_n=\min_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\), then the upward-closed convex set
\(D_n=C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) contains \(v_n\mathbf1\), while
\((v_n-a)\mathbf1\notin D_n\) for \(a>0\).  To construct a supporting
normal directly, let \(y_k=(v_n-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) and let \(d_k\) minimize
\(\|y_k-d\|_2\) over \(d\in D_n\).  Existence follows by restricting the
closed set to the compact ball centered at \(y_k\) with radius
\(\|y_k-v_n\mathbf1\|_2+1\).  Convexity and minimality, applied to
\(d_k+s(d-d_k)\) and differentiated at \(s=0+\), give
\[
 (d_k-y_k)^\top(d-d_k)\geq0
 \quad(d\in D_n).
\]
Put \(\lambda_k=(d_k-y_k)/\|d_k-y_k\|_1\).  Since
\(D_n+\mathbb R_+^M=D_n\), substituting \(d=d_k+ae_j\) shows
\((\lambda_k)_j\geq0\); hence \(\lambda_k\in\Delta_M\).
Along a convergent subsequence, \(\lambda_k\to\lambda_n\in\Delta_M\).
Moreover \(d_k\to v_n\mathbf1\), because \(v_n\mathbf1\in D_n\) and
\(\|d_k-y_k\|_2\leq\|v_n\mathbf1-y_k\|_2=\sqrt M/k\).
Passing to the limit in the projection inequality gives
\(\lambda_n^\top(d-v_n\mathbf1)\geq0\) for all \(d\in D_n\).  Thus
\[
 \inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
 =\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{21}
\]
Indeed, support gives the inequality from right to left, while
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\) gives the reverse inequality.  Translating
regret vectors by the oracle vector yields
\[
 V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\}.
\tag{22}
\]
The same finite-dimensional argument for diffusion risks gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\right\}.
\tag{23}
\]
It follows from (19)--(23) that
\[
 |V_n-V|
 \leq
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 +\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{24}
\]

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  By (20) and (24), choose \(N\) sufficiently large
that
\[
 |V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3.
\tag{25}
\]
Choose \(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
 \max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\tag{26}
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) from
(1).  Exact equality of its scenario-risk vector and (25)--(26) gives
\[
 \max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{27}
\]
Thus \(u^\epsilon\) is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.

We finally approximate this particular control for the original
discontinuous loss.  Conditional on the exogenous randomization and on any
action sequence having positive conditional probability, the sampled
Gaussian block increments are absolutely continuous on their sampled
coordinate subspace.  A terminal threshold equality is a zero set of
\[
 \sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\tag{28}
\]
If at least one coordinate \(j_0\in I\) was sampled, condition on all
sampled Gaussian coordinates except \(X_{j_0}\).  Equation (28) then has
at most one solution for \(X_{j_0}\), because
\(\exp(X_{j_0}-Q_{j_0}/2)\) is strictly increasing; the conditional law of
\(X_{j_0}\) has a density, so the conditional probability of equality is
zero.  Fubini's identity makes the unconditional probability zero.  If none
was sampled, its left side is
\(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).  There are finitely many \(I\), so
\[
 \Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
 \text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{29}
\]

For horizon \(n\), divide enrollment into \(N\) consecutive blocks whose
lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the subgroup selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout each block, and supply its normalized Gaussian block
aggregate to the next decision kernel.  This rule is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\).  The block clock lengths
converge to \(1/N\), and the aggregates have their exact Gaussian laws;
induction over the fixed number \(N\) of blocks gives terminal-state
convergence to \(u^\epsilon\).  Measurable decision kernels can first be
modified on sets of arbitrarily small probability, simultaneously under
the finite family of Gaussian history laws, so that the induction is
performed at continuity points.  By (29), for each \(a>0\) there is an open
neighborhood of the finitely many threshold surfaces whose probability is
below \(a\).  Off that neighborhood the terminal loss is continuous, while
its absolute value is at most one.  Weak convergence on the closed
complement, followed by an error of at most \(2a\) and then
\(a\downarrow0\), gives predictable policies
\(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfying
\[
 L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
 \quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{30}
\]
Equations (27) and (30) prove the asserted risk-vector transfer.  The
construction allows zero block allocations.  Every step used only the
declared finite list and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); null-boundary closure was not
used.

We prove the assertion first for a generic one of the two experiments.
Let \(\mathcal A\) denote its policy class and write
\[
 r(a)=\bigl(L(a,1)-c_1,\ldots,L(a,M)-c_M\bigr).
\tag{31}
\]
In the finite experiment every symbol in (31) is given its \(n\)-subscript.
Because each loss belongs to \([0,1]\) and \(c_m\) is its infimum over
policies,
\[
 0\leq L(a,m)-c_m\leq1.
\tag{32}
\]
Hence
\[
 C=\overline{\{r(a):a\in\mathcal A\}}\subset[0,1]^M
\tag{33}
\]
is compact.  Time-zero exogenous randomization, permitted in
\(\mathrm{def{:}finite\mbox{-}policy\mbox{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\), makes \(C\)
convex.

Put \(v=\min_{r\in C}\max_mr_m\) and
\(D=C+\mathbb R_+^M\).  Compactness supplies \(r^\star\in C\) with
\(r^\star\leq v\mathbf1\), so \(v\mathbf1\in D\).  For every \(a>0\),
\((v-a)\mathbf1\notin D\) by the definition of \(v\); consequently
\(v\mathbf1\) is a boundary point of the closed convex upward set \(D\).
For a direct separation argument, let
\(y_k=(v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\notin D\), let \(d_k\) be its Euclidean
projection onto \(D\), and normalize
\(d_k-y_k\) to have coordinate sum one.  The projection exists by
closedness after restriction to a sufficiently large compact ball.
Minimality along every segment from \(d_k\) to \(d\in D\) gives
\[
 (d_k-y_k)^\top(d-d_k)\geq0.
\]
Upward closure shows every coordinate of \(d_k-y_k\) is nonnegative.
Also \(d_k\to v\mathbf1\), because \(v\mathbf1\in D\) and
\(\|d_k-y_k\|_2\leq\sqrt M/k\).  A convergent subsequence of the normalized
vectors therefore has a limit \(\lambda^\star\in\Delta_M\), and passage to
the limit gives
\[
 {\lambda^\star}^{\!\top}r\geq
 {\lambda^\star}^{\!\top}(v\mathbf1)=v
 \quad\text{for every }r\in C.
\tag{34}
\]
Conversely, \(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\) for every
\(\lambda\in\Delta_M\).  Therefore
\[
 v=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\min_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{35}
\]
Closure does not change the infimum of a continuous linear functional.
For the finite experiment,
\[
 \inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r
 =B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m},
\tag{36}
\]
whereas for the diffusion experiment it equals
\[
 B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m.
\tag{37}
\]
Equations (35)--(37) are the two displayed minimax identities in the
theorem.  Further, by (32),
\[
 \left|\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r-
 \inf_{r\in C}{\lambda'}^\top r\right|
 \leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
\tag{38}
\]
The dual objective is therefore continuous on compact \(\Delta_M\), so a
least-favorable prior is attained in each experiment.

\emph{Posterior-state reduction.}
Fix \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\).  Under the zero-drift reference law, the
scenario-independent observed control contributes identical assignment
factors under every scenario.  Conditional Gaussian likelihood
calculations give, at every \(t\),
\[
 Z_m(X(t),Q(t))
 =\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
 -\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}.
\tag{39}
\]
Because \(Z_r>0\) and at least one \(\lambda_r>0\), the denominator below
is strictly positive.  Bayes' formula therefore gives
\[
 \Pr_\lambda\{m\mid\mathcal F_t\}
 =\frac{\lambda_mZ_m(X(t),Q(t))}
 {\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r(X(t),Q(t))}
 =b_m^\lambda(X(t),Q(t)).
\tag{40}
\]
The same change of measure gives
\[
 \sum_m\lambda_mL(u,m)
 =\mathbb E_0^u\!\left[
 \sum_m\lambda_mZ_m(X(1),Q(1))
 \ell_m(X(1),Q(1))\right].
\tag{41}
\]
Thus the Bayes problem has terminal cost determined by
\((X,Q,b^\lambda)\), and its controlled transition law is determined by
\((t,X,Q)\) and the current simplex action.

The approximation and Markovization steps require uniform integrability of
the likelihoods.  The proof of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}boundary\mbox{-}stable\mbox{-}frontier}\), equations
\((6)\)--\((11)\), established by the pathwise factorization
\(Z_m^2=\mathcal E(2M_m)_1e^{\langle M_m\rangle_1}\), the bound
\(\langle M_m\rangle_1\leq H^2\), and the bounded-energy
conditional-Gaussian argument, proves that
\[
 \sup_{u\in\mathcal U,\,1\leq m\leq M}
 \mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2]\leq e^{H^2}.
\tag{42}
\]
In particular, (42) does not condition on, or assert independence of, the
adaptive clock.

For a simple observed control on a finite time partition, disintegrate each
action at a decision time conditional on the state
\((X(t),Q(t),b^\lambda(t))\), and use that conditional simplex vector as
the randomized Markov action.  Induction through the conditional Gaussian
transition kernels preserves the state distribution at every later
decision time and hence the terminal reference-law distribution.  Simple
predictable controls approximate every admissible control as in the proof of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}boundary\mbox{-}stable\mbox{-}frontier}\).  On each
partition the randomized Markov kernels take values in the compact simplex;
diagonal weak compactness over rational times yields a limiting relaxed
Markov kernel.  The bounded affine drift and covariance identify its limit
with the limiting Gaussian martingale problem.  The uniform \(L^2\)
estimate (42) transfers the limiting reference terminal-state equality to
all scenario risks through (41).  Hence every admissible risk vector is
matched by a relaxed control Markov in
\[
 \bigl(t,(X_j(t),Q_j(t))_{j\in\mathcal J},
 (b_m^\lambda(t))_{m=1}^M\bigr).
\tag{43}
\]

\emph{Existence and the saddle response.}
For completeness, we verify attainment in the diffusion problem.  Clock
paths satisfy
\[
 0\leq Q_j(t)-Q_j(s)\leq t-s,\qquad
 \sum_jQ_j(t)=t,
\tag{44}
\]
and score martingales have total quadratic variation at most one in each
coordinate.  The induced relaxed-control laws are tight.  Any weak limit
retains the Gaussian martingale problem because drift and covariance are
bounded and affine in the simplex action; the class is therefore compact
after the time-zero randomization already allowed by \(\mathcal U\).
The map \((x,q)\mapsto a_j(x,q)\) is continuous, and consequently
\(\mathbf1\{a_j(x,q)<0\}\) is lower semicontinuous.  In the reference-law
representation (41), each likelihood factor is continuous and positive and
each summand is nonnegative.  Approximate each nonnegative
lower-semicontinuous terminal summand increasingly from below by bounded
continuous functions.  Weak convergence applies to each approximation;
taking first the sequence limit and then the monotone approximation limit
shows that the expectation at the limiting law is no larger than the
limiting inferior of the expectations.  The \(L^2\) bound (42) removes
likelihood truncation uniformly.  Hence the Bayes terminal cost is
lower-semicontinuous along relaxed-control limits.
Thus every diffusion Bayes problem has an attained minimizer.  The same
argument applied to the finite maximum of the lower-semicontinuous scenario
regrets gives an attained minimax control \(u^\star\) such that
\[
 r_m(u^\star)\leq V\quad(m=1,\ldots,M).
\tag{45}
\]

Let \(\lambda^\star\) be an attained least-favorable prior in the diffusion
experiment.  Equation (34) states that every admissible control \(u\)
satisfies
\[
 \sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u)\geq V.
\tag{46}
\]
Applying (46) to \(u^\star\) and using (45) gives
\[
 V\leq\sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u^\star)\leq V.
\tag{47}
\]
Thus \(u^\star\) is a Bayes best response to \(\lambda^\star\).
Markovization in (43) preserves its entire risk vector, so this best
response may be chosen Markov in the state stated in the theorem.

Regard this one control as a finite mixture with one component.  It is an
exact saddle response and hence, for every \(\epsilon>0\), an
\(\epsilon\)-saddle response:
\[
 \sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u^\star)\leq V\leq V+\epsilon
 \quad\text{for every }\lambda\in\Delta_M,
\qquad
 \sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u)\geq V
 \quad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.
\tag{48}
\]
Taking \(\lambda=e_m\) in the first inequality yields
\(r_m(u^\star)\leq V+\epsilon\) for every scenario \(m\).  The argument
uses only the finite-dimensional simplex of the arbitrary finite scenario
list and the coordinate bound \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); it does not require
null-boundary closure.

prose_updates.tldr: For any declared finite bounded list of local causal-effect scenarios, the fixed arithmetic-mean closed e-test admits an adaptive subgroup-recruitment minimax-regret frontier. Exact Gaussian grid embedding and a quantitative terminal-envelope comparison transfer the discontinuous closed-test risk, including zero-allocation faces, to and from the controlled score diffusion. Finite-scenario convex duality yields an attained least-favorable prior and posterior-state Markov response. A deterministic nested interval Bellman search supplies convergent certified bounds without a closed-form mesh rate. Null-boundary closure is optional application structure, not a theorem premise; global comparison at arbitrary off-origin boundary states remains open.

project_justification.gap: Existing enrichment designs optimize a chosen-prior utility or a discretized finite-stage program, while existing adaptive-experiment diffusion results principally transfer regular payoffs. They do not establish boundary-stable value and policy transfer for the discontinuous rejection vector of a fixed closed e-test on an arbitrary finite bounded scenario list with legal zero-information faces, nor do they provide a validated primitive-input interval certificate for that frontier.
project_justification.niche: Holding the confirmatory test and its established error guarantee fixed isolates the design problem of adaptively recruiting among prespecified subgroups. The local Gaussian score experiment then becomes an auditable finite-scenario robust-control problem for causal treatment-effect scenarios, with no forced-exploration premise and no need to close the scenario list under null-boundary projections.
project_justification.fill: The project proves exact grid embedding, a quantitative boundary-stability modulus, uniform Bayes and oracle convergence, minimax-regret convergence, predictable finite-policy attainment, and an attained least-favorable-prior posterior-state reduction. It also proves termination of a deterministic nested certificate search whose explicit error ledger validates both the value interval and a recovered policy mixture.

prose_updates.related_work: Adusumilli's 2025 diffusion-control theory supplies the nearest Bayes and minimax architecture for regular data, and Adusumilli's 2026 allocation-process representation supplies a broad finite-to-continuous donor; the present theorem adds the discontinuous closed-test payoff transfer on arbitrary finite bounded scenario lists. Wager and Xu provide the weak-signal score-clock construction for regular state-dependent randomization. Burnett and Jennison and Ballarini et al. study prior-weighted enrichment under frequentist error control, whereas the present finite-scenario saddle selects an adversarial prior for minimax regret. Rosenblum, Fang, and Liu motivate sparse finite-stage optimization, and Baas, ter Schure, and van Rosmalen motivate scalar e-value dynamic programming; neither supplies the present nested lower-and-upper validation with an independent recovered-policy check. The fixed strong-FWER and confidence-sequence corollaries continue to rest on the cited e-merging, closed-testing, Ville, and time-uniform inversion results.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proved frontier and saddle results assume known unit Gaussian variance, finitely many prespecified disjoint subgroups, positive normalized missed-discovery weights, the fixed elementary e-alternatives and arithmetic-mean closure rule, and an arbitrary finite scenario set contained in a bounded local-effect cube. No lower bound on subgroup allocation is imposed. Null-boundary closure may be adopted as an application convention but is not used by the theorems or the certificate instance. The certificate is qualitative and computable at every positive tolerance; no closed-form mesh size, arithmetic complexity bound, convergence rate, or nontrivial interval-certified numerical run is claimed. Unknown variance, delayed responses, overlapping or data-discovered subgroups, and optimization of the confirmatory test are outside scope. Global generalized-terminal comparison and uniqueness at viable off-origin boundary states remain open.

statement_notes.justification: It identifies the attainable local-power regret frontier for the fixed confirmatory test on every finite bounded scenario list and transfers a near-optimal diffusion risk vector to predictable finite-stage recruitment.
statement_notes.gap: The regular-payoff diffusion results of Wager and Xu and Adusumilli do not themselves handle this discontinuous closure payoff. The theorem supplies the boundary-stable envelope transfer while allowing zero-allocation faces; the corrected likelihood argument controls adaptive clocks by stochastic-exponential factorization rather than an invalid independence equality.
statement_notes.consumer: It converts a continuum recruitment solution into asymptotically equivalent finite-stage policies for interAdapt-style subgroup-enrichment designs.

statement_notes.justification: The least-favorable prior converts robust enrichment into a posterior-state control problem while the saddle inequalities certify every scenario regret simultaneously.
statement_notes.gap: Prior-weighted enrichment methods take the prior as an input. This result derives an attained adversarial prior and a Markov Bayes response whose complete risk vector is minimax, for an arbitrary finite bounded scenario list.
statement_notes.consumer: It supplies robust scenario weights and a posterior-state policy response that can populate a confirmatory trial design specification.
